title: Shopping in shops that have no 'shops'

breadcrumb.text: Shopping in shops that have no 'shops'

body.text: 29 July 2016

Arguably the biggest change to shopping in the 20th century was the emergence of supermarkets. For many this made the shopping experience less personal, but as online shopping has become the norm for many in the 21st century, shopping has, to some, become even less personal; in 2008 just 5p of every £1 spent in shops was spent online – by 2015 this had risen to 13p.

body.h4: Spending in online shops broken down by shop type, Great Britain, 2015
body.text: So, nearly half of every £1 spent in shops online in 2015 was spent in online stores that have no permanent physical presence on the high street or out of town shopping park. These shops might have a stall sometimes in a market or fair, but that’s it. This is not a blip – it’s actually a growing trend – up from 41p of every £1 spent in shops online in 2010.

body.h3: So what does this mean for British shopkeepers?
body.text: So what does this mean for British shopkeepers?

body.h3: So what does this mean for British shopkeepers?
body.text: Well, considering that nearly 88% of all shopping in Great Britain in 2015 was done in physical stores it’s clear that the British public are not ready quite yet to move to an exclusively online shopping experience. However, it could be that some shop types will become more online focused than others in the future, as it does seem that there are some items we are more willing to buy online than others.

body.h3: So what does this mean for British shopkeepers?
body.text: Looking at physical shops that also have an online presence, only 4p of every pound spent in shops mainly selling food was spent online, whereas 12p of every pound spent in clothing stores was spent online and 11p of every pound spent in department stores.

body.h3: So what does this mean for British shopkeepers?
body.text: This might have something to do with delivery and returns. When ordering food to be delivered you have to ensure you are at home for the delivery – this is not so for clothing items. Also, it can be difficult and time consuming to return food but lots of clothing stores have made it free and very easy to return their products by making it possible to drop packages off at the corner shop for example, or using lockers in supermarkets.

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: The November effect on online shopping

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: One of the most intriguing trends over recent years has been growth of online shopping in November. There is a spike in our overall spending in online shops in that month.

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: In 2008, 6% of all shopping in November was carried out online, rising to 16% in November 2015.

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: While people spend more overall online and in store in December than November, the advent of online sales events like [Cyber Monday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyber_Monday), which take place in November, and the increasing convenience of online shopping, has seen people seemingly using online buying as a chance to get organised early for Christmas.

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: All statistics here are based on retail sales excluding spending on fuel.

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: Retail is divided into the following sectors:

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: food stores – these are supermarkets, specialist food stores and stores that sell alcoholic drinks and tobacco (summarised as “Shops that mainly sell food” here)

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: department stores

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: textiles, clothing and footwear stores (summarised as “Clothing shops” here)

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: household goods stores, such as those selling electrical items and furniture

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: other stores, such as those selling jewellery, toys, sporting goods and books

body.h3: The November effect on online shopping
body.text: non-store retailing, which includes retailers with no physical stores, mail order, catalogues and market stalls.
